items.note: Kramrisch: prescribed sacrifices and offerings before and after a temple is built, with Vastupurusha appeased by the renewed rite of Vastusanti; canonical background for temple building.
The rite of Vastusanti and the building activity are performed together by priest (sthapaka), architect (sthapati) and builder (karaka).
Quoted prescription from the Vastupurusha myth: whoever builds a divine or human residence should first worship Vastu; temples and houses built without Vastu worship are 'demon's work'.
Kramrisch's interpretation: the goat-Asura, swelled by pride, sinks down and the gods take their stand on him and the temple is built; plan leads to the centre, elevation to the upper worlds.

reject_reason: string of textual citations on the recumbent position of the Vastupurusha; no usable evidence for Udaypur or a specific temple feature

items.note: Quotes the Samarangana-sutradhara (XIV.2) for the Vastupurusha's head in the East in a 64-square site, and in the North-East in an 81-square site.
Kramrisch: the temple ground plan is laid out in analogy with the Vastupurusha mandala, garbhagriha square at the centre (Brahmasthana), thick walls, buttresses from the zone of the 32 Padadevatas.
The temple ground plan, whatever its variations, is analogous to the Vastupurusha mandala and its rhythm derives from the Vastumandala.
Sculptures on temple walls reflect the same relation; their iconography is essentially iconometry (talamana) resting on proportion and position.

reject_reason: mythic variants and Puranic citations about the Vastupurusha; no direct bearing on a unit

items.note: Story in the Isanasivagurudevapaddhati: the goat-headed Asura begs Siva for residence (vastu) and becomes Vastupa, protector of site and building; name from root 'vas'.

Footnote: the Vastupurusha remains an Asura with both Deva and Daitya roles; he is Vastu-brahma, created first by Viraj or, per the Samarangana-sutradhara (II.4), by Brahma by whom the worlds were created afterwards.
Brahma stands in the heart of the Vastu; Manu Smriti prescribes an offering in the centre of the building to Brahma and Vastospati together.
From inception to completion of a building the indwelling divinity is worshipped; quoted rule to begin with Vastu worship and end with that of the Vasus.

Kramrisch's symbolic reading: man sets up the temple on the appeased Vastu as 'the monument of his own transformation'; superstructure points to the primeval descent and is undone by the ascent along the temple's body.
The temple is dedicated as the residence of divinity (Mahanirvana Tantra).
Vastupurushamandala of 64 or 81 squares for Brahmanas and Kshatriyas; forty-five Devatas occupy the body, number unchanged between plans.
Centre is the place of Brahma with 44 Devatas around; the Brahmasthana covers four squares in the Manduka plan and nine in the Paramasayika plan.
Inner rim of 12 Devatas and outer rim of 32 Padadevatas (Prakara Devatas) around the central Brahmasthana: 1+12+32.
Reference table cites the Samarangana-sutradhara XI.21-25 for the Manduka A plan.

items.note: Twelve inner and thirty-two outer gods are placed around Brahma at the centre; the Brahmasthana alone remains an unchanged square in the 64 or 81 square Vastu.
Brahma always stands in the middle of the Vastupurusha, whether the head lies east or, as is more general, north-east.
Footnote: the majority of texts, including the Samarangana-sutradhara, place the Vastupurusha with head in the north-east.
